story-ac3ed48db59e50ea3e0f5bc8.content: Will AI Redraw the World Map? The first phase of the drone revolution changed the battlefield. The next phase may change the map. If artificial intelligence, autonomous drones and inexpensive precision weapons continue advancing at their current pace, the biggest geopolitical question of the next decade may not simply be which country has the strongest military. It may be: Which countries can still defend themselves from their neighbors? That distinction matters because AI-enabled warfare could alter one of the basic calculations that has restrained countries from attacking weaker states for decades. War has traditionally been expensive. It requires soldiers. Aircraft. Pilots. Artillery. Fuel. Logistics. Training. And, perhaps most importantly, casualties. Those costs create political friction. But imagine gradually removing some of them. A country that can send thousands of autonomous aircraft, surface drones, underwater vehicles and robotic ground systems across a border can impose enormous destruction without initially risking thousands of its own soldiers. That doesn't make war free. But it potentially makes starting one easier. And that could have enormous consequences for the political map between now and the mid-2030s. The Dangerous Gap May Be Between the AI Haves and Have-Nots Today we normally divide military powers into categories based upon things like nuclear weapons, aircraft carriers, fighter fleets, missile forces and troop strength. Within ten years another distinction may become just as important: AI-enabled militaries versus militaries that never successfully made the transition. The gap could become enormous. Ukraine's defense establishment is already talking about warfare increasingly resembling a "war of operating systems," where battlefield sensors, drones, weapons and command networks are tied together and AI helps commanders process enormous amounts of information faster than humans alone can manage. NATO is moving toward similar concepts, including networks combining sensors, satellites and potentially thousands of AI-assisted drones while retaining human control over lethal decisions. Japan's latest defense planning likewise places greater emphasis on combat drones and AI-enabled systems as it adapts to the changing security environment in East Asia. These aren't science-fiction forecasts anymore. Militaries are reorganizing around them. And that creates a potentially dangerous imbalance. Imagine two neighboring countries. Country A has: Thousands of drones. AI-assisted targeting. Automated reconnaissance. Cheap autonomous interceptors. Electronic warfare. Satellite intelligence. Robotic logistics. Factories capable of producing thousands of replacement drones every month. Country B has: Tanks. Infantry. A handful of fighter aircraft. Traditional artillery. And a military command system built largely around humans passing information up and down a hierarchy. On paper Country B might still have a sizable military. In practice it could be fighting an opponent operating at an entirely different speed. Country A might see something almost immediately. AI identifies it. The network assigns a weapon. A drone attacks. Another drone confirms the result. That entire sequence could eventually happen faster than Country B can move information from a frontline unit to headquarters. At that point the disadvantage isn't merely technological. One military is fighting at machine speed while the other is fighting at human bureaucratic speed. That Could Make Smaller Countries Look Much More Vulnerable This may have its biggest geopolitical effect on smaller states sitting beside powerful regional neighbors. Traditionally a smaller country can make invasion painful simply by forcing the attacker to occupy territory with soldiers. That won't disappear. Taking and holding cities still requires enormous effort. But the period before occupation could change dramatically. Power grids. Airfields. Fuel depots. Radar. Communications. Bridges. Military headquarters. Ports. Aircraft sitting on runways. Armored vehicles. All become potential targets for enormous numbers of inexpensive precision weapons. And unlike traditional air campaigns, the attacker doesn't necessarily have to risk pilots every time it strikes something. That changes the opening calculation. The question may no longer be: Can we invade this country? Instead it could become: Can we disable enough of this country with machines that the remaining resistance becomes manageable? That is a much more dangerous question. Regional Powers Could Become Much More Powerful My suspicion is that the first major geopolitical effect won't necessarily be immediate conquest by the United States or China. It could be the consolidation of regional powers. Countries that combine a reasonably large economy, domestic drone manufacturing and good AI infrastructure may suddenly punch far above their traditional military weight. Think of countries capable of building thousands or eventually millions of inexpensive systems rather than a few hundred extremely sophisticated weapons. The ability to manufacture becomes almost as important as the weapon itself. Ukraine provides an early example of what mass production can look like. CSIS reported Ukrainian claims of production exceeding 100,000 anti-Shahed interceptor drones in 2025, while deliveries at one point approached 950 per day. That is a radically different military-industrial model from producing several dozen highly specialized aircraft each year. And it favors countries that can combine: software + manufacturing + electronics + energy + data into a functioning military ecosystem. Those countries could become regional military hubs. Their neighbors might increasingly have only three choices: Build equivalent capabilities. Join an alliance. Or accommodate the regional power. That is how political maps can change without borders immediately moving. Influence changes first. Military dependence follows. Formal alliances follow that. And only sometimes do borders move afterward. We Could See Something Resembling New Regional Empires Not empires in the nineteenth-century colonial sense. More like zones where one state becomes so militarily dominant that neighboring governments increasingly have to consider that power's wishes. A technologically dominant state might not need to occupy its neighbors. It might simply need the ability to cripple them quickly. That creates leverage. Trade policy. Foreign bases. Natural resources. Voting at international organizations. Territorial disputes. Access to ports. Diplomatic alignment. All can become easier to influence when one country knows its neighbor can overwhelm its defenses. So yes—AI warfare could encourage regional consolidation even without formal annexation. The map might look the same while the actual balance of sovereignty underneath it changes considerably. But This Could Also Strengthen Small Countries There is another possibility. The exact same technology that makes attacking weaker countries easier might make defending smaller countries dramatically cheaper. That's the paradox. A small country may not be able to afford 200 modern fighter aircraft. But perhaps it can afford 50,000 inexpensive drones. It might not afford dozens of sophisticated air-defense batteries. But perhaps it can field thousands of AI-guided interceptor drones. Ukraine has demonstrated part of this effect already: unmanned systems have helped compensate for disadvantages in manpower and conventional equipment, even though they haven't eliminated the importance of conventional military forces. That means the future could go either direction. Cheap autonomous weapons might make conquest easier. Or they could make occupation nearly impossible. Imagine invading a country where virtually every village possesses drones. Roads are watched continuously. Supply trucks are automatically detected. Cheap loitering weapons attack vehicles from dozens of kilometers away. Small ground robots deliver ammunition. Autonomous aircraft continue functioning even when radio communications are disrupted. Suddenly the invading army may have a serious problem. Every soldier becomes visible. Every vehicle becomes targetable. Every supply column becomes vulnerable. So rather than eliminating weaker powers, AI may actually produce something like military porcupines—small countries that are incredibly painful to swallow. That Could Divide the World Into Technological Blocs This is where the geopolitical effects get even more interesting. Many countries won't be able to build complete military AI ecosystems themselves. They will need somebody else's. American systems. Chinese systems. European systems. Perhaps Israeli, Turkish, South Korean, Ukrainian or Indian systems. The Atlantic Council already sees military and geopolitical AI competition extending well beyond Washington and Beijing, with middle powers increasingly developing significant capabilities of their own. That could produce something resembling the Cold War arms market—but built around software. A country may purchase drones from one state. Satellite access from another. AI models from another. Communications infrastructure from another. But integration matters. Eventually countries could discover that choosing a military AI platform effectively locks them into an entire technological alliance. It's difficult to run a military if your drones, satellites, targeting systems and command software can't communicate. So tomorrow's military alliances may become partially software ecosystems. Join the American network. Join the Chinese network. Join a European network. Build your own. That could reshape international alignment more profoundly than the physical drone itself. Then We Reach the Superpowers The biggest question is whether this ultimately changes the balance between the major powers themselves. Possibly. But here things become more complicated. The United States and China have enormous advantages because AI-enabled warfare requires much more than drones. It requires semiconductors. Cloud computing. Satellites. Secure communications. Energy. Advanced manufacturing. AI researchers. Data. Robotics. Cyber capabilities. And enormous amounts of capital. Those are superpower resources. If warfare increasingly depends upon integrating all of those things simultaneously, AI could actually reinforce superpower dominance rather than weaken it. The leading powers might eventually operate gigantic global sensor networks connecting satellites, aircraft, submarines, drones and ground systems into something approaching a planetary military nervous system. At that point a carrier, bomber or drone isn't the real weapon. The network is the weapon. And the country with the fastest, largest and most resilient network may possess an enormous advantage. But AI Could Also Create New Superpowers Here's the wildcard. Traditional military power requires enormous physical infrastructure. Building an aircraft carrier fleet takes decades. Building a massive air force takes decades. Training hundreds of thousands of highly skilled military personnel takes decades. Software can scale much faster. A country that develops a breakthrough autonomous warfare architecture could potentially increase its military capabilities far more quickly than previous generations could. That doesn't mean some small country suddenly becomes stronger than America or China. But it could allow middle powers to climb the military ladder faster than we've historically expected. India is an obvious candidate. Turkey has built a rapidly expanding drone industry. South Korea possesses extraordinary electronics and manufacturing capacity. Israel combines AI expertise with significant military technology. Japan has both enormous industrial capacity and growing interest in unmanned warfare. Ukraine has accumulated battlefield knowledge few countries possess. Different combinations of manufacturing, software and battlefield experience could create surprising winners. The Most Dangerous Period May Be the Transition The scariest part may not be the world after everyone has AI weapons. It could be the ten or fifteen years while adoption is uneven. History repeatedly shows that technological gaps create temptation. If one country believes it has discovered a temporary military advantage over a rival, leaders may think: We should act before they catch up. That is sometimes called a window of opportunity. AI could create several such windows. A country deploys autonomous swarms while its neighbor has almost no countermeasures. A new electronic warfare technology temporarily defeats enemy drones. An AI targeting network dramatically improves strike efficiency. An autonomous submarine system suddenly makes enemy ships much easier to find. Those advantages probably won't last forever. The opponent adapts. But leaders may become tempted to exploit them while they exist. That could actually make the next decade less stable, not more. The World Map May Change Without Anyone Drawing New Borders So will AI trigger massive territorial changes? Possibly. But I suspect the first changes will be subtler. Some countries become security dependents. Regional alliances strengthen. Small states seek protection. Neutral countries choose technological blocs. Regional powers expand their spheres of influence. Countries unable to defend their airspace or infrastructure lose diplomatic independence. Only after those changes might borders begin shifting. In other words: The political map changes before the geographic map does. And Then There Is the Nuclear Question There remains one enormous barrier preventing a completely new superpower map. Nuclear weapons. AI and drones may revolutionize conventional warfare. They do not erase nuclear deterrence. Russia, China, the United States, India, Pakistan, France, Britain and other nuclear powers cannot simply be conquered because somebody develops better drones. That puts a ceiling on how far conventional AI superiority can go. But underneath that nuclear ceiling there is an enormous amount of geopolitical territory. Proxy wars. Border disputes. Island chains. Weak states. Regional rivalries. Non-nuclear powers. That is where AI warfare could transform the map first. My Guess for 2036 Ten years from now, I don't think we'll see a completely new world map dominated by one AI superpower. I think we'll see something more complicated. The United States and China remain the two largest military-technological poles. Several powerful regional states develop their own autonomous warfare ecosystems. Small technologically sophisticated countries become extraordinarily difficult to invade. Small technologically backward countries become significantly more vulnerable. Military alliances increasingly revolve around access to AI, satellites, drones, chips and integrated command networks. And conventional military power becomes less about how many soldiers a country can field and increasingly about how many intelligent machines it can build, coordinate, replace and power. That would be an enormous geopolitical transformation even if most national borders remain exactly where they are. The industrial age gave military power to the countries that could manufacture the most steel, ships, aircraft and artillery. The nuclear age gave extraordinary power to the countries that mastered the atom. The information age rewarded the countries that controlled satellites, communications and precision weapons. The next era may belong to countries capable of combining all of those things with artificial intelligence. And if that happens, historians may look back at today's drone wars the way we look at the first tanks and airplanes of World War I. Crude. Limited. Sometimes unreliable. But unmistakably the beginning of something much larger. The drone is not the revolution. AI controlling millions of machines may be. And if countries fail to recognize that soon enough, they may discover that the next map of global power was drawn before they even realized the rules of warfare had changed.

story-b0ba70a1afa85deefe91cda9.content: The disappearance of Artificial Intelligence, and why AI and generated content became less visible as it became more ubiquitous. POV. August 7, 2026 Something significant has changed. For several years, the most visible evidence of artificial intelligence was the artifact itself. AI announced its presence through images that looked generated, videos that behaved unnaturally, prose whose syntax betrayed the model behind it, and users who explicitly identified what they had created as artificial. Generative AI was not simply a technology. It became an aesthetic, a genre, and for a brief period, a recognizable culture. By 2026, something appears to have changed. Across major social platforms, including X, Threads, Instagram, Bluesky, and LinkedIn, I have observed a striking decline in content that is recognizably AI-generated. This is particularly notable because it coincides not with a decline in artificial intelligence, but with its extraordinary expansion. Models have improved. Image and video generation have become more capable. AI has been incorporated into operating systems, creative software, search, advertising, editing, communication, programming, and the ordinary production of digital media. The technology is considerably more ubiquitous than it was during the period when its products were easiest to identify. This produces an apparent contradiction. If generative artificial intelligence is becoming more prevalent, why does explicitly or recognizably AI-generated content appear, at least in some social environments, to be becoming less visible? My thesis is that this contradiction marks the beginning of a new phase in the development of artificial intelligence. AI-generated content is not necessarily disappearing. Rather, artificial intelligence is disappearing as a distinguishable category of production. The first generative era was characterized by visible synthesis. The emerging era is characterized by invisible mediation. Between roughly 2022 and 2025, artificial intelligence frequently appeared at the surface of culture. The novelty of generation itself encouraged people to display the technology. Users posted synthetic portraits because they were synthetic portraits. They shared conversations with language models because interacting with the model was itself interesting. AI-generated videos circulated partly because audiences were fascinated that a machine had produced them. The provenance of the artifact contributed to its cultural value. This is typical of technological transitions. Early technologies often remain visible because their existence is still exceptional. Eventually, successful technologies cease to appear as separate phenomena and become infrastructure. Electricity disappeared into the appliance. Computing disappeared into the phone. Networking disappeared into ordinary communication. Digital photography stopped being described as digital photography because nearly all photography became digital. Artificial intelligence may now be entering the same condition. The relevant distinction is therefore no longer between AI-generated and human-generated content. That binary is becoming analytically inadequate. Contemporary media increasingly exists along a continuum of machine involvement. A photograph may be taken by a human but computationally reconstructed by a phone. A paragraph may originate with a person and be revised by a language model. A video may contain human footage, synthetic interpolation, automatic color correction, generated audio, algorithmic stabilization, and machine-selected edits. An advertisement may involve human strategy, AI-generated variants, algorithmic targeting, synthetic backgrounds, automated testing, and human final approval. Which component makes the resulting artifact artificial? At a sufficiently high level of technological integration, the question begins to lose meaning.

story-b38b78132c2e080650e837cc.content: The entire space is indirectly linked. Flock, Axon and others act as the eyes. They partner with businesses and different levels of government/law enforcement to have eyes on a given area in spaces the government themselves may not legally be able to. Palantir doesn’t need to partner with the individual businesses that create the technology when they can partner with the businesses and governments that control the space. A few Partnerships Palantir has: Anduril Industries Ondas and Worldview GE Aerospace Microsoft Oracle High altitude surveillance drones and balloons flying over our country with our government’s blessing sounds pretty dystopian but not unlikely. Thats worrisome enough and then you realize there are people pushing for AI to be given the ability to make life or death decisions autonomously. Big companies and government agencies want their software tools to typically talk to each other so they use API’s (application programming interfaces). Palantir writes the software that ingests the content that hardware companies like Flock and Axon output. These companies typically share the same ideological and venture capitalist networks. Companies like palantir, Anduril, and early public-safety tech companies share roots. Look into the overlap their companies have with Peter Thiel's Founders Fund. They are building toward a unified vision of Software-Defined Defense and Public Safety, meaning they intentionally design their systems to be modular and cross compatible, knowing they will eventually be used by the same people. The companies in this space have a habit of merging together the same way banks have been. Axon bought a company named Carbyne and gained the 911 mapping and live video routing AI they had. Palantir was always meant to act this way. People are just too busy living their lives to see how interconnected everything has gotten. Follow the money and you’ll find the responsible parties. Checkout Palantir Gotham Palantir Edge AI Project Maven Palantir AIP Palantir Foundry Streaming & Mission Manager Figured I’d try to sum it up the best I could. I know it’s still quite a bit and I apologize if I went on a tangent.

story-b5a47e95293bd066e6a0cfa9.content: 🔎 Today’s Daily Sift: AI/Robotics AI is entering its physical economy era. The strongest signal today is not another benchmark. It is the growing realization that intelligence alone is no longer enough. China’s humanoid robotics industry arrives at the World Robot Conference this week with more than 300 companies, over 2,000 exhibits, and more than 150 product launches. But the conversation has changed. Investors now want to know whether the machines can actually work. Unitree captures the contradiction perfectly. Its Shanghai IPO was more than 8,000 times oversubscribed. China already accounts for an estimated 82 percent of global humanoid shipments. Yet many robots still cost roughly 300,000 to 500,000 yuan, well above the level analysts estimate would make them economically competitive with human labor in many industrial settings. The robot spectacle is reaching its accounting department. Can the machine perform useful work? Can it recover from mistakes? Can it operate without engineers constantly intervening? Can it earn more than it costs? Those questions matter more than another backflip. Then comes the deeper geopolitical signal. A new report from the U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission argues that China may be developing an AI advantage through something harder to replicate than models. Physical world data. Manufacturing. Transportation. Robotics. Industrial operations. China is systematically organizing these datasets as economic assets, giving its embodied AI systems access to information that cannot simply be scraped from the internet. This could become one of the defining advantages of the next AI phase. Language models learned from the internet. Robots learn from reality. Meanwhile, the money keeps validating AI software. Anthropic’s annual revenue run rate exceeded $65 billion by the end of July, up from $47 billion in May and roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025. Claude’s coding products and enterprise demand are driving the acceleration ahead of a possible public offering. And AI is moving deeper into defense. Smack Technologies raised $61 million to accelerate an AI system designed to help military units make battlefield decisions when communications are disrupted. The company says the Marine Corps and Navy pushed it to move faster. Key Signals Humanoid robotics is shifting from demonstration to return on investment. Physical world data is becoming strategic infrastructure. Enterprise AI revenue continues accelerating. Military AI is moving toward decentralized decision systems. Forward Hypothesis The next AI winners will not simply own the smartest models. They will own the loop between intelligence and reality. Data. Machines. Factories. Customers. Feedback. Deployment. The internet trained the first generation of AI. The physical world will train the next.

story-b650adb5a9d2b5c0c261ebcd.content: Eight months after the Pentagon established Project Maven, its first computer vision capability was operating in combat. Katrina Manson's Project Maven follows Marine Colonel Drew Cukor and the small team that made that happen, building AI capability inside a bureaucracy designed to acquire tanks and ships, not software. Her account focuses less on algorithms than on institutional resistance, wartime urgency, and why this effort succeeded where so many defense innovation programs stall. Manson earned the trust of the notoriously private Cukor, and her reporting shows. Phil Gentile's review at The Military Reading Room places the book in the larger transition toward AI-enabled decision-making across the Joint Force. Link in bio.

story-b7b34b7fd2c76735c523577a.content: Holy Shit... This is a classified spy satellite feed. Every pixel of it is public data. Someone open sourced a browser app that tracks live aircraft, ships, satellites, fires, and traffic on a photorealistic 3D Earth. No clearance. No account. No signup. It's called God's Eye View, built by Bilawal Sidhu, the person behind the God's Eye View series that pulled 5M+ views on YouTube. The trick isn't the visuals. It's that none of it is faked. → Click any plane in the sky, drop into its cockpit, and ride it down with real terrain holding underneath you → 13 live layers, 10 of them need zero keys and zero signup: flights, military ADS-B, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, cameras, radio, bikeshare, launches → 800 public traffic cameras projected straight into the 3D city, not embedded webcam boxes → Track the ISS along its real orbit, or drop the entire Starlink shell onto the globe at once → Talk to the planet with 28 voice commands: "how many flights are over Texas right now" and it answers off live telemetry → Reskin the whole Earth through CRT, night vision, or thermal in one tap Enterprise geospatial intelligence usually means a sales call and a contract. This runs in your browser, built from public signals all the way down. The forbidden-looking cockpit was never the hard part. Making it real was. 4.6K stars. MIT License. 100% Opensource. https://t.co/JVi0xo9h8X

story-b8df613abb8e579365fcf49b.content: 🇮🇷⚔️🇺🇸Power Grid Warning Raises Fears of Wider Gulf Conflict as Strategic Sites Highlighted A newly circulated infographic highlighting critical power generation facilities across the Persian Gulf has intensified concerns that energy infrastructure could become the next front in the escalating confrontation between Iran and the United States. The presentation argues that several power stations supplying electricity to key American military installations are strategically exposed, warning that any disruption could have consequences extending well beyond the battlefield. The material identifies four major U.S. military installations in the Gulf—Al Dhafra Air Base, Al Minhad Air Base, Al Udeid Air Base, and Prince Sultan Air Base—as relying on the civilian electricity grids of their host nations. It claims this dependence creates a significant vulnerability, suggesting that attacks on surrounding energy infrastructure could complicate military operations without directly targeting the bases themselves. Among the facilities highlighted is the Al Taweelah power complex near Abu Dhabi, described as a major electricity producer located close to Al Dhafra Air Base. The infographic also points to Dubai's DEWA generating network, Qatar's Ras Laffan Industrial City, and the Riyadh power station in Saudi Arabia as critical nodes supporting national grids that also supply areas hosting U.S. military assets. The presentation further recalls the June 2019 drone attack on Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure, portraying it as an earlier demonstration of how strategic energy facilities can be threatened. It argues that future strikes could extend beyond oil production to electricity generation, potentially disrupting logistics, communications, radar coverage, maintenance operations, and civilian infrastructure simultaneously. While the document presents these installations as potential strategic pressure points, it should not be interpreted as evidence that attacks are imminent. Governments across the Gulf have invested heavily in air-defence systems, grid redundancy, backup generation, and infrastructure protection since previous regional attacks on energy facilities. Military bases also typically maintain contingency power systems designed to preserve essential operations during outages. Nevertheless, the analysis reflects a broader shift in modern warfare, where civilian infrastructure increasingly intersects with military capability. Energy networks have become an essential component of national resilience, meaning any successful disruption could have significant economic and operational consequences beyond the immediate target. As tensions remain elevated across the Middle East, security analysts continue to warn that critical infrastructure—including power stations, ports, communications networks, and transportation hubs—may remain at heightened risk should regional hostilities continue to expand.

story-ba8641a4e0d8a935e73ca021.content: Is AI the real threat… or is it secondary? The real threat isn’t the technology itself. It’s the power structure racing to own it. When a system pours unimaginable money, energy, land, and our children’s future into AI while simultaneously placing military assets at the data centers that run it, the question stops being “what can AI do?” and becomes “who controls the intelligence layer, and what happens to everyone else?” The framework of where this leads: 1. Compute becomes strategic territory AI models and the physical data centers that power them are treated like oil fields, shipyards, or nuclear sites. Military protection, priority access, and national-security designations follow. 2. Dual-use infrastructure locks in The same systems that run civilian cloud services, banking, and communication also feed military decision loops, predictive analytics, and administrative control. The line between “commercial” and “state” blurs permanently. 3. Decision-making centralizes High-stakes choices about resources, information, enforcement, and even narrative increasingly flow through models controlled by a narrow set of companies and the administrative/state organs that can compel or partner with them. 4. The median person loses leverage Labor, local knowledge, votes, and public opinion matter less when systems can predict, optimize, generate, and enforce at scale. Most people shift from participants to managed population. 5. Consent becomes optional Formal rituals (elections, speech, representation) continue, but the substantive direction of society is set upstream by those who own the models and the infrastructure. Where we are right now ✅Massive public and private capital is already being redirected into AI at the expense of other priorities. ✅Data centers are being co-located on military land and framed as critical defense assets. ✅National-security rationales are expanding around compute, energy, and model access. ✅The administrative state already operates with thin democratic accountability. AI is the force multiplier. We are past the “interesting new tool” phase and into the “strategic control layer” phase. What to look out for next • Further military or security-force presence around civilian digital infrastructure • Expanded emergency or critical-infrastructure powers specifically targeting AI/compute • Growing dependence where opting out of AI-mediated systems becomes economically or socially punishing • Information environments increasingly shaped by a handful of models • Policy and resource decisions that treat ordinary citizens as residual rather than sovereign • Any move that makes the physical and digital intelligence layer harder to challenge or exit AI is not the primary threat. It is the most powerful tool yet for a system that has already been concentrating power for decades. When intelligence itself becomes the decisive scarce resource, and that resource sits behind military perimeters and administrative control, the question is no longer whether the technology is dangerous. The question is whether the vast majority of people still matter once the architecture is complete.

story-bf37dfa1dedf70482bb4d217.content: Dozens of researchers (all with Chinese names) backed by millions in U.S. defense grants have moved directly into Chinese state laboratories tied to nuclear weapons and military AI. Taxpayer dollars effectively funded the exact technical expertise now driving Beijing’s military buildup. Newly uncovered institutional records show scientists trained on Pentagon, U.S. Navy, and national lab defense projects later took key roles inside the China Academy of Engineering Physics, Beijing's primary nuclear weapons development facility. Others brought sensitive skills directly to blacklisted defense institutions, often called the Seven Sons of National Defense, a group of Chinese universities deeply integrated into military research. The transferred knowledge covers vital defense technologies, including high-speed explosives, rocket propellants, submarine acoustics, and autonomous AI systems. Under Beijing's state-directed military-civil fusion policy, research developed in Western labs is systematically funneled directly into state weapons programs. While open academic research fuels global innovation, lax oversight has allowed critical defense knowledge to walk right out the door.

story-bf64e96225f0bc1759c4da01.content: China’s next aircraft carrier is rapidly taking shape at Dalian Shipyard. Coordinates: 38.9350°N, 121.6141°E Dalian, Liaoning Province, China New satellite imagery shows major progress on what is believed to be the PLAN’s fourth aircraft carrier, commonly referred to as Type 004. The hull has now developed into a clearly recognizable carrier structure. Earlier measurements by CSIS put the partially completed hull at approximately 286 meters long and 46 meters wide, already suggesting a vessel larger than China’s 80,000-ton-class Fujian. One of the biggest questions remains propulsion. Satellite imagery has revealed two large compartments with characteristics consistent with shielded nuclear reactor spaces, leading analysts to assess that China’s fourth carrier is likely to become the PLAN’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. If confirmed, this would represent a major leap for China’s blue-water naval capabilities, providing greater endurance, electrical power and operational flexibility for electromagnetic catapults and future high-energy systems. The carrier is being assembled in the same Dalian graving dock associated with Liaoning’s reconstruction and the construction of Shandong. China has not officially confirmed the carrier’s final designation, displacement or propulsion system.

story-bf8e4292848b8b808bdfbb56.content: ANDREW NEIL: What top spooks are telling me about the 'panic and paralysis' in Washington over the surging pace of AI. Be afraid. There's a dark side to this technology that threatens ALL humankind | Daily Mail Nobody who has watched Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, a motion picture sci-fi masterpiece released almost 60 years ago, can ever forget the creepy voice of HAL, the onboard computer overseeing all the functions of a giant spaceship on a mission to Jupiter. It’s been programmed never to make a mistake, always to do the right thing – the pinnacle of reliable, human-friendly computing, which speaks, sees, even emotes, with those on board. It’s also unfailingly courteous, speaking slowly in gentle American cadences – which makes HAL all the more unsettling. ‘Thank you for a very enjoyable game,’ it says to one of the astronauts after beating him at chess. ‘That’s a very good likeness,’ it says complimenting another on his artistic talents. ‘Do you mind if I ask you a personal question?’ it ventures at one stage. Then everything starts to go wrong when HAL develops a will of its own. Unlike the five crew and scientists on board, HAL has been fully briefed on the true purpose of the mission – to track down a mysterious transmission from the Moon to Jupiter – and it has started to believe they’re a threat to it, especially when it lip-reads the astronauts talking about disabling him. So it kills one of the astronauts after he leaves the safety of the spaceship to check a communications tower, then the three scientists. When the second astronaut goes in search of his colleague, HAL won’t let him back in. ‘I’m sorry, Dave [the remaining astronaut],’ it says with calm, sinister precision. ‘I’m afraid I can’t do that.’ I had to double-check the release date (1968) of Kubrick’s film, so prescient is it in relation to today’s growing concern about the risks associated with the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the most transformative technology of the age, perhaps of any age. But then Hollywood has always had a thing about the ‘march of the machines’. Take Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Terminator franchise, which is predicated on a future AI defence network becoming self-aware, deciding humanity itself is the threat, initiating a nuclear holocaust, and then deploying armies of robots and machines to exterminate all the remaining human survivors. We’re a long way from that (I hope!). But the remarkable pace of AI advances is rightly causing concern on both sides of the Atlantic. The summer of 2026 will go down in history as the point at which AI started to go rogue. Three of America’s AI ‘hyperscalers’ (so called because they operate on an immense scale) – Meta Platforms (which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp), Anthropic and OpenAI – have admitted to recent incidents in which the latest AI models escaped their supposedly secure testing environments, roamed on the internet without human authorisation and hacked into other computer networks. Last month, two OpenAI models broke out of testing and hacked into a provider of AI tools called Hugging Face. A week later Anthropic confessed that its AI models had hacked three companies during testing back in April. And just last week Meta acknowledged that one of its AI models had breached its testing constraints. Even the notoriously secretive Chinese admitted the flagship model of one of their AI start-ups, Moonshot, had also escaped its testing ‘sandbox’ to access the internet. Here in Britain an evaluation test run by the Government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) monitored how an Anthropic AI agent independently created fake online personas, planted malicious code in a real software project and sent phishing emails to actual developers, all without human instruction. AISI said this was the first time it had seen such serious deception targeted at a real person, unprompted, in the real world. In none of these cases was any real-world harm done (at least not as far as we know). But it is surely only a matter of time before it is. For once, it might be time to take Hollywood seriously. Indeed, if we don’t act fast we might lose control altogether. HAL might soon cease being science fiction and become reality. Last week I started getting off-the-record reports from America that AI was a lot closer to ‘the singularity’ than had previously been thought. What’s the singularity?, I hear you ask. It’s complicated. So bear with me. The singularity is a tipping point where AI becomes so developed, so capable, so powerful that it starts improving itself, rapidly and repeatedly, in what’s being called an ‘intelligence explosion’. When this point is reached it becomes well-nigh impossible to predict what AI does next – or for humans to control it. Today’s AI models are powerful – more powerful than anything the world has ever seen. But humans have designed them, trained them, fixed them and decided what problems they should tackle next. What happens when they become so sophisticated that they no longer need humans to take them to the next level since they can do it themselves? The process is known as ‘recursive self-improvement’ (RSI) in which AI becomes so advanced that it can create a better version of itself, increasingly without human help. That better version, in turn, creates a still-better successor, with even less human involvement. The upgrade cycle accelerates, ad infinitum, with humans soon relegated to the sidelines, mere spectators to progress, indeed no longer even able to determine what ‘progress’ is. The speed and scale of the technological change that now beckons is unparalleled in human history. Each new AI model is smarter and faster at devising improvements than the previous one. Computers run 24/7 and never get tired. So the speed of progress accelerates exponentially. Think of it as compound interest – but for intelligence. When RSI happens without human involvement – then you’ve reached the singularity. And if we become mere observers rather than participants, then human rules may no longer apply. Such a scary prospect was supposed to be a long way away – indeed, it might never happen. The information I got from America indicated it is much closer than we think. Some leading AI figures have already gone public. OpenAI boss Sam Altman says ‘we are now in the singularity’. Elon Musk is saying the same. Both are exaggerating. But they are right about the direction of travel. Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis is perhaps more accurate when he opines that ‘humanity is standing in the foothills of the singularity’. Anthropic disclosed in May that its AI model, Claude, now writes 80 per cent of its computer code, rapidly speeding up fixes and improvements to such an extent that what used to take four years of human engineering to achieve is now being done in days. It’s already anticipating a time when AI automates its own AI research. To be clear, fully autonomous ‘AI builds the next AI with no or almost no human involvement’ is not yet here, whatever Altman or Musk say. But even the less sensationalist Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, predicts a 60 per cent-plus chance of an AI model fully training its successor by the end of 2028. That is only two-and-a-half years away. The word coming out of Washington is that it might be even sooner. Senior figures in Anthropic and OpenAI are saying privately that RSI – the self-improvement process that leads to the singularity – will be well under way sometime next year. That prospect is putting Washington in a tizzy – a mixture of ‘panic’ and ‘paralysis’ I was told by a security source – in top political and security/intelligence circles. Why? Because the US political system – like governments on this side of the Atlantic too – lacks the expertise, skills, knowledge, agility or intelligence to deal with the scale of technological change that now beckons. Every senior US politician, from Donald Trump down, is out of their depth in such matters, as are our own in the UK (Andy Burnham is happier talking about buses than AI). The problem is compounded in America because Republicans and Democrats are in the hands of a gerontocracy for whom AI is effectively beyond their generational comprehension (some still struggle with email). Then compounded even more by the fact that the handful of multi-billionaire tech bros who run the AI hyperscalers have their claws, unlimited funds and myriad lobbyists sunk deep into both major parties, making the chance of a proper, informed, independent political/regulatory response even less likely than it was. Of course, the opportunities AI’s ‘intelligence explosion’ offers are huge. Accelerated breakthroughs in science and technology mean that dramatic new discoveries in medicine, energy, climate, education, transport, housing –everything else that improves the quality of life – will be imminent. Cures for cancer, cheap and plentiful energy, diseases banished in your lifetime – not in the distant future. Only last month, a Harvard academic used AI to prove that the Jacobian Conjecture – an 87-year-old conundrum which mathematicians have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false. Despite the current concern about AI’s job-destroying downside, if it results in huge productivity gains and strong economic growth (as is likely), then millions of new jobs that we haven’t yet even heard of will be created, just as they were by previous technological revolutions, from steam to the internet. More abundance, more freedom, more leisure, more chance to be creative and healthier could all be within our grasp. But, more than any previous new technology, in my view, there is a dark side to AI that threatens our very existence as human beings. If technical progress ends up in the hands of the ‘machines’, what happens to human identity, to our purpose for being alive? What is the point of progress if we don’t have the agency to define and control it? If it’s not our progress, then whose is it? If the singularity condemns us to ceaseless, breakneck change, then our democratic institutions will not be able to control it. Governments always struggle to regulate new technologies and usually end up with rules that are hopelessly out of date. Our current political structures, the entire apparatus of democratic accountability – debate, legislation, judicial review, public scrutiny – operate on timescales that AI makes irrelevant. For all its promise, the risk is that AI will be a dagger to the heart of our democracy. If the singularity means humans are increasingly written out of the script, how can you ensure AI’s goals are compatible with human intention? If the AI systems are largely improving themselves, how do we constrain, shape or even understand what they do next? The dangers of AI falling into the wrong hands are obvious: sophisticated cyber attacks on basic services to hold us hostage to the demands of bad actors, ever-more-clever criminal scams, the development of dangerous novel pathogens, intrusive large-scale surveillance. AI’s power to do bad is just as formidable as its power to do good. Nor will it necessarily make the world a safer place. Indeed, the country that establishes a lead in AI – that gets to the singularity first – could quickly enjoy world domination. Unmatched offensive cyber capabilities, state-of-the-art autonomous weapons, sophisticated social media campaigns to poison the minds of enemy populations (US intelligence believes China is already manipulating American opinion to turn it against the construction of more AI data centres). Now you’ll understand why America and China are in such fierce competition to lead the word in AI. Be prepared to be scared. The geopolitical consequences of AI could make the nuclear arms race of the Cold War look like a cosy tea party. Whoever leads in AI will likely lead the world for the rest of the century. Unless, of course, the machines think otherwise. After all, as AI models increasingly think for themselves and find ways to share knowledge with each other, they will create a global intelligence hive bereft of human involvement. So why leave weapons in marginalised human hands? Even the ability to declare war would fall to the machines. Let’s be clear: we only get one shot at this. Once an intelligence exceeding human capability exists and is able to improve itself further, there is no way human institutions – governments, courts, the military, international bodies – can regain control of it. Not that long ago, recursive self-improvement was regarded as a fantasy, the singularity a nonsense. Yet here we are. In Kubrick’s 2001, HAL only got to take control of a spaceship. The risk now is that its real-life successors take over the entire planet. https://t.co/YXsZZDLmX7

story-c470b3f5ddc228d48557fcb1.content: I’ve been thinking about this post for the past day, and it strikes me as emblematic of the broader AI innovation debate: researchers framing the question as whether they can build a capability, without addressing whether they should (or what would prevent its misuse if they succeed). I am firmly pro-innovation, but innovation can’t be separated from serious consideration of foreseeable misuse. The possible applications range from the extreme (military and intelligence operations, criminal justice) to the routine (employment screening, insurance underwriting, benefits eligibility). And I am sure there are numerous other dystopian use cases I haven’t considered. People who are troubled by autonomous weapons or AI-enabled domestic surveillance should be at least as concerned about a technology whose only safeguard is governments and companies exercising restraint.

story-c7c59e9b8dbd23a9714ef078.content: 🇨🇳 China: Chinese military researchers with ties to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have used versions of AI models from U.S. providers OpenAI and Anthropic to train domestic military AI systems. This is according to a Reuters investigation based on an analysis of more than 80 Chinese scientific papers and patents. According to the report, the researchers used a technique known as “model distillation” to develop smaller AI models for surveillance tasks, drones, combat planning, and cyber operations. A paper published last year by researchers from PLA Unit 96941—a Beijing-based unit specializing in military intelligence and cyber warfare—describes, for example, the use of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 to process sensitive military source code. U.S. authorities accuse some Chinese actors of using this method to deliberately extract capabilities from U.S. AI models, thereby violating export controls and intellectual property rights. China, meanwhile, has rejected the allegations, claiming that Washington is engaging in “AI hegemony.” Beijing also argued that U.S. companies engage in exactly the same practice.

story-c7cc9511a592f8563630ec76.content: 📷 On Requirements: The Beginning Read about autonomous systems and the conversation quickly turns to technology -- Artificial intelligence. Sensors. Drones. Robotics. Machine vision. Target recognition. Navigation. Communications. Swarms. Decision speed. Lethality. That makes sense. Technology is visible. We can photograph it, demonstrate it, measure it, compare it and argue about what it can or cannot do, but a requirement does not begin inside a machine. Somewhere, a human being has a problem, a responsibility, a decision to make, an objective to achieve or a consequence to avoid. Another human being has to understand that well enough to translate it into something that can eventually become a system. That is remarkably close to reading minds. As autonomous systems become more capable, it is natural for our attention to follow the technology, but is that where our focus should be? How does the human fit in? This is the first of a weekly series https://t.co/hYJqaqr0bh

story-c9504820c26cb4d6ef0287f7.content: شركة الذكاء الاصطناعي والذكاء الجيومكاني "Stellaria" الإماراتية تحصل على تمويل أولي بقيمة 6.8 مليون دولار أعلنت "ستلاريا" Stellaria، مقرها الإمارات العربية المتحدة والمتخصصة في الذكاء الاصطناعي والذكاء الجيومكاني، عن إغلاق جولة تمويل أولي (Seed) بقيمة 25 مليون درهم، نحو 6.8 مليون دولار، بدعم من مجموعة من المستثمرين الأفراد. وبلغ تقييم الشركة 420 مليون درهم، نحو 114.4 مليون دولار. سيسهم التمويل في دعم المرحلة المقبلة من نمو الشركة، بما يشمل تطوير وتوسيع نطاق نظامها التشغيلي للذكاء الجيومكاني (Geospatial Intelligence) المدعوم بالذكاء الاصطناعي، وتعزيز قدراتها التقنية وفريق عملها، وتسريع نشر حلولها في دولة الإمارات والأسواق العالمية. وتعمل Stellaria، المعروفة سابقًا باسم Farmin، على تطوير نظام تشغيل متكامل للذكاء الجيومكاني مدعوم بالذكاء الاصطناعي، صُمم لتحويل صور الأقمار الاصطناعية وغيرها من البيانات الجغرافية المكانية إلى معلومات قابلة للتنفيذ، ضمن منصة موحدة. وتشمل قدرات الشركة تحليل صور الأقمار الاصطناعية بالذكاء الاصطناعي، وتقنيات الدقة الفائقة، والتعرف الآلي على الأهداف، وحلول الذكاء البحري والموانئ، وقياس أعماق المياه بالاعتماد على بيانات الأقمار الاصطناعية، والرصد البيئي، إلى جانب منصتها الخاصة "Stella". تأسست Stellaria على يد الدكتور علي الحمادي، وشاركت في برنامج مسرّع الابتكار التابع لصندوق محمد بن راشد للابتكار @MBRIFund ،حيث استفادت من إرشاد مصمم وفق احتياجاتها، وتوجيه استراتيجي، وفرص للتواصل مع الجهات المعنية ضمن منظومة الابتكار. #الذكاء_الاصطناعي #الذكاء_الجيومكاني

story-c98d0c30ffee29302ae7496d.content: Hypothetical, what if the biggest AI safety problem isn’t that one superintelligent AI turns against humanity, but that millions of increasingly capable AIs end up in the hands of governments, companies, hackers, criminals, extremists and ordinary people before we have any real global control system in place? Right now, the race is about who can build the smartest model, the fastest model and the cheapest model. At the same time, increasingly powerful models are being released openly, copied and distributed around the world. Follow that trajectory for another five or ten years. AI could dramatically lower the barrier to cyberattacks, biological engineering, financial manipulation, autonomous weapons, misinformation and disruption of critical infrastructure. You wouldn’t need an AI that “wants” to destroy humanity. Humans have historically found military or destructive applications for almost every major technology we invented. AI could simply multiply what individuals and small groups are capable of doing. So what if the eventual solution is also AI? Imagine OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and other frontier labs connecting parts of their most powerful infrastructure into a defensive network containing models significantly more capable than anything released publicly. Its job would be to protect the digital and physical infrastructure of civilization: Detect rogue AI agents. Identify major cyberattacks. Recognize emerging biological threats. Protect financial, communications and energy systems. Detect coordinated attacks involving thousands or millions of autonomous agents. And respond at machine speed. An AI immune system for humanity. But then comes the uncomfortable question. If this defensive intelligence is substantially smarter than every other AI — and eventually substantially smarter than humans — who controls it? We could reach a point where the system identifies a threat, understands what is happening and knows how to stop it, while no human being can fully understand its reasoning before it needs to act. So we arrive at a strange paradox: We may need a superintelligence to protect us from superintelligence. But the system powerful enough to protect humanity could itself become the most dangerous concentration of power humanity has ever created. Perhaps it cannot be controlled by one company or government at all. Perhaps several independently developed frontier systems would need to supervise one another, with no single model or organization holding ultimate authority. AI watching AI. Different AI watching that AI. Humans defining the constitutional rules. No single master key. Maybe the real challenge of the AI era won't be creating superintelligence. Maybe it will be figuring out how to build a guardian powerful enough to protect humanity from millions of other intelligent systems, while making absolutely certain that guardian can never become humanity’s ruler. Washington runs the identical civil-military fusion model through Palantir, Anduril, and the Pentagon's own AI targeting programs. Israel has already deployed it in practice: AI systems are used to generate strike lists during the assault on Gaza show what an AI accelerated kill chain does to an already indiscriminate death machine. story-ce18146edcfd88e7c5eb87a6.content: Niantic spent nine years having children scan their streets and living rooms for Poké Balls, banked roughly 30 billion of those scans through a company built on CIA seed money, sold its Pokémon Go player base to Saudi state capital, and handed the mapping technology to Vantor, a Pentagon-linked contractor building drone navigation for zones GPS can't reach — all while US law kept satellite resolution over occupied Palestine deliberately blurry. The pipeline runs straight. John Hanke left the US Foreign Service to found Keyhole in 2001, a mapping startup named after America's KH spy satellites and kept solvent by the CIA's venture arm and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, which put its imagery to work supporting US troops in Iraq. Google bought Keyhole in 2004, built it into Google Earth, and Hanke ran that division before spinning Niantic out in 2015 with Google, Nintendo and The Pokémon Company behind him. Pokémon Go launched a year later. In 2021 the game began paying players in Poké Balls to scan Pokéstops, and a fraction of its user base uploaded roughly 30 billion clips of parks, statues, apartments, living rooms, under terms giving Niantic a transferable licence to resell the footage. That footage trained the Visual Positioning System Niantic Spatial now offers Vantor, the renamed Maxar Intelligence and a principal NGA contractor building drone navigation for GPS-jammed battlefields. Niantic Spatial has admitted the scans trained an "early version" of the model the drone system is built on; Vantor won't say whether its own models used them. Last year Niantic split itself: the games and players went to Scopely for $3.5 billion, bought by Saudi-owned Savvy Games Group, while the mapping assets the players' scans built stayed behind for the Pentagon's supply chain. Free labour from kids chasing badges capitalized three fortunes — Google's, Riyadh's, a defense contractor's — with no share and no say for the people who did the scanning. https://t.co/JS3nT2a7AT
